utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Defence would raise a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. And we should do this one outside the presence of the witness, I think. The Defence is addressing Your Honours to obtain guidance to see how to most effectively proceed with the proceedings and to ensure that fairness is upheld for the Defence. Last night, we received from the Prosecution several e-mails from their -- that they had received from their expert witness Dr. Clark and included in the e-mails are several photographs from -- I believe from the autopsies at Tomasica which were being disclosed for the first time to the Defence. And so I have photographs now that to me, as an untrained layperson, I can't draw conclusions from them and know what to ask in re-direct, because I no longer have access to my forensic pathologist to tell me what is important and what isn't. And since they were not disclosed to the Defence previously, we did not have a chance to go over those photographs during the proofing prior to the testimony. So in that instance, then I would ask for at least, at the very at least after the Prosecution's cross is completed to be able to consult with the expert as to the photographs, to see if there's anything that I need to ask in re-direct arising from the photographs because we did not have an opportunity to do so prior. And I guess the bigger question, then, is how many other photographs relating to the autopsies at Tomasica does the Prosecution's expert have which were never given to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the Prosecution like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. After the testimony where Dr. Stankovic mentioned that he didn't think six bullets could be in the head at the end of the day, I spoke to Dr. Clark and mentioned that to him and he responded that he had photographs of that. And I said, Okay, can you send them to me. So he did, and we passed them on to Mr. Ivetic and put them on our list for cross-examination. And that's where we are. I have no objection to Mr. Ivetic having a chance to talk with Dr. Stankovic about it, perhaps after cross-examination would be, I think, our preference, but certainly he should have a chance to do that. It's not something that it was in our possession beforehand. I just -- we learned about it after the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it just about one or more photographs about six bullets in the head or is there more?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's two other photographs on the issue of -- you may remember Dr. Stankovic talked about a difference between Dr. Clark's opinion on the path of a bullet through a skull versus the Muslim pathologist's opinion that thought it took another path. And so there was a couple of pictures on that that Dr. Clark also sent. He'd had a chance to look at some of the testimony online.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think that was on a case where the cause of death was undetermined by both experts. No, both -- no, both damage to the head. I mean, they were united on that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's right. I think I remember you asking about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we are talking about a limited number of photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the present situation. I think when Dr. Clark was here, no doubts were raised in relation to the six bullets in the head at the time, but the matter has been raised now, and the Chamber thinks that it's in the interests of justice to have some additional material. But, at the same time, the Chamber thinks that it's also a requirement of fairness that the Defence would have an opportunity to briefly discuss it but then after cross-examination so that -- that we'll be best informed about possible disagreements between the parties and what the factual basis for that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. But we also have the issue of -- we don't know what other photographs of these remains that Dr. Clark has in his possession. He has picked two. That's my problem, that I don't know what the universe is of other photographs. I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, have you disclosed all the photographs you received from Dr. Clark recently to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All the photos we got from Dr. Clark recently we disclosed, and we didn't have any before that, as far as I know. And I'm told Dr. Clark mentioned that he -- in his report that he took photographs and no one seemed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To bother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- to bother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you have fulfilled your disclosure obligation in this respect. Whether Dr. Clark has any more or not, Mr. Ivetic, we don't know. Mr. McCloskey apparently has not asked him. I think during his examination it was not asked to him either, whether he would make them available, yes or no. So that's where we stand at this moment in respect of availability and disclosure of photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then if you consult with Professor Stankovic after the cross-examination, it should be limited to those photographs, nothing else. I hope that that's clear for you and we'll tell Dr. Stankovic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. MacDonald. You find Mr. MacDonald to your right. Mr. MacDonald is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor I'd like to discuss with an issue with regard to your autopsies in Zvornik in 1992. Now, on Monday, at transcript page 43275 to 43276, you testified that you went to Zvornik twice, once on 30th April and once on 5th May 1992, and you performed autopsies on the bodies of Muslims that had been found in and around Kula. You also said that documents from those autopsies were in the possession of the special court and that you were actually a witness in the case against Grujic et al. I'd just like to confirm the timeline here, professor. You performed the autopsies in 1992. What year did you testify against Grujic et al?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was in 2013 or 2014 at the Special Court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, if I can have 65 ter number 25862, I'm just going to try to refresh your memory, Professor Stankovic. And we should have the indictment here against Grujic et al. And just to stay on the first page, it's just the date that I'm looking for. We see that it's the district court in Belgrade, war crimes chamber. We see the indictment against Grujic is the first name accused and then there are six others, including Branko Popovic, and it's dated 12th August, 2005. So that it was the years -- the immediate years following that indictment that you testified?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said 2013 or 2014, unless I'm mistaken. So it was at some point after the year 2000 that I testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Have you testified in any other case against Grujic et al?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was just this one single case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And are you aware of any other proceedings that you were taken against Branko Grujic and the others, apart from this case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that there were others, but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at temporary transcript page 34 to 35 yesterday, during a discussion over your claim regarding people shot after they were already dead, you gave the example of Zvornik and you went on to say: "In principle, we did not have special teams that carried the bodies of those who lost their lives in armed conflict. It was the other combatants who were present and who then transported the bodies." Now, I'd like to clarify this as well, professor. You were testifying in this case against Grujic et al because you performed the autopsies on the victims in that case. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And those victims hadn't died in armed conflict; they were, in fact, murdered, or at least some of them were murdered. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot talk about that. I talked about the injuries and the cause of death of these people and whether they died in armed conflict or whether it was a consequence of something else, it is not up to me to determine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 33754, please. We're just looking at the first page in both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This is the judgement at first instance against Branko Grujic and Branko Popovic. On the page there, you'll see judgement, the accused, and the first name in bold is Branko Grujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And if we can go to the second page in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And all I'm looking for here, you can see the second accused name in bold, Branko Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in both languages -- sorry. Before we do, you'll see the words "are guilty" and then "of having." And if we go to the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Under the number I, we see: "As per a prior arrangement and joint decision, on two occasion, they took hostage civilians, men of Muslim ethnicity fit for military service." And then later on in the text in the bold, we see: "Forcibly displaced on 26 June 1992 the Muslim population of the village of Kozluk."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, if we can move, please, to page 13 in the English and page 10 in the B/C/S, and here the judgement is discussing -- sorry. If we can go back one page in the English. My apologies. Page 12 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And there at number 2, and you see it in the B/C/S as well, is the charge or the count, "Failure to take measures to protect the hostages taken." And it starts: "During the period from 29th May up until approximately 1st July, 1992," and it talks about 162 hostages confined at Dom Kulture. And if we now turn the page in the English, please, to 13. We stay on the same page in the B/C/S and just where you see the indented paragraphs, we see the name Dusan Vukovic, and it says he killed 16 and wounded 20 persons. The next paragraph, Dragan Slavkovic, for killing two persons. And there are a number of other persons in the last indented paragraph. And, finally, if we can turn over the page in the B/C/S and move to page 14 in the English, I'm looking for the number 100. It's about ten pages down in the English -- ten lines down, sorry, and it's about midway down the first paragraph in the B/C/S. And it states around 100 persons were killed in this way. So, Professor Stankovic, I just wanted to clarify this matter that was perhaps raised that potentially the bodies that you autopsied were killed at armed conflict. This judgement is quite clear that at least some of the bodies you autopsied that you were testifying about in this judgement, they were -- they were murdered?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if you look at the indictment for the period when these people were killed, that was significantly later than the time when I performed autopsies. I performed the autopsies on the 30th of April and the 5th of May, 1992. All these events, as follows from the indictment, occurred at a later time. Therefore, I couldn't have performed autopsies on people who had already -- who had still been alive. The 27th of May is mentioned here, so all the victims perished after the date. I did not examine their bodies, and I cannot comment on that. I performed autopsies on some other people about a month earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. I'll perhaps come back to that point later, Professor Stankovic. I'd now like to turn to a discussion you had with Mr. Ivetic over the meaning of a Latin term.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we have D00283 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, you may remember seeing this document on Monday.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to refresh Your Honours' recollection, we probably shouldn't view this to the public because of the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm obliged to my friend. And, Your Honours, before we get into a discussion about the Latin term, I wonder if I might make a suggestion which is that the booths instead of interpreting the Latin words when I say them rarely simple say the Latin term itself, just to avoid any confusion or potential confusion in interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think if the booth have understood this and it's not really interpretation but I hope your Latin is still good enough. Mine might not be. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic at transcript page 42936, you were asked what could cause that kind of injury that this Latin diagnosis describes. And you stated fragmentation of mines or explosive such as mortar shells or cannon shell and hand-grenades. Now, just to let you know the Prosecution agrees that wounds inflicted by these kind of devices can be described with a diagnosis, vulna explosiva. But what I'd like to suggest to you that wounds inflicted by a gun can also sometimes be described as vulna explosiva. Would you agree with that, Professor Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what are the gun-shot injuries that could fit within the diagnosis of vulnar explosivum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to show you a couple of examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And just before I do, Your Honours, for orientation in terms of the case, the reason that I'm discussing this term is because of the significance of the survivor of the Jadar river massacre, which you may recall came up in 98 bis. Just to let you know that I'm not going into a discussion about Latin language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That I'm not going into this discussion for no reason. If we can have 65 ter number 33694, and I'm looking for page 2 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, what you are about to see is a medical report of an injury a person has sustained. Now, I realise it's harder to read in the B/C/S than in the English but the first line of the English and first line of the B/C/S, it states: "The patient was admitted on 31 August 1993 at about 1930 hours because of injury inflicted by sniper shot to the head." And if we look further down the page at the diagnosis, and I think this is easier to read in the B/C/S it's about midway down, you see: "V explosivum reg occipitalis."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I was just waiting for the transcript. Now, I understand that means an explosive injury to the part of the head just behind the ear. Is that what that diagnosis means?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: So now this is an example of a doctor who being told that the injury was inflicted by a gun still described the wound as vulnera explosivum. Now, you said you wondered what kind of weapons or guns could fit into that diagnosis. An injury from a sniper rifle, could that fit in? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. An injury inflicted by a sniper bullet may only be diagnosed as vulnus sclopetarium. Obviously this is either ignorance of the doctor who gave the diagnosis because obviously he does not distinguish between gun-shot injuries and blast injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If he can move to another example, 65 ter 33695, and it's the first page in both languages that I'm looking for. And in about the middle of the page in a box we see the words: "Diagnosis on admission, v. explosivum haemithoracic l. dex." Now, the haemithoracic cavity, that's one part of the chest. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's either the right side or the left side of the chest. Either the left or the right side. Haemithoracic means either the right side or the left side. It means half of the chest area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you for that. If we look down at the description of what happens three sentences down in both languages, you see the words: "Injuries sustained from a sniper bullet to her chest." Now, Professor Stankovic, I take it you would then say that the diagnosis v. explosivum is again being used in error given that this is it a gun-shot wound?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The medical document in Serbian or the Bosnian-Herzegovinian is not good. The diagnosis in English states: "Vulnus explosivum, haemithoracic lat dex." That's one diagnosis and that means a blast wound in the right side of the chest area. Underneath that, the second diagnosis is: "Vulnus transclopetarium reg brachii l. dex," which means a gun-shot wound in the area of the right upper arm. There are two founds, one is a blast wound in the right side of the chest and then there is gun-shot wounds inflicted by a projectile from a hand fire-arm in the right upper arm area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I certainly appreciate that the right -- I think it may be the bicep has the diagnosis v. transclopetaria, but the diagnosis of the chest wound v. explosivum being linked to the sniper bullet to the chest I take it you would say that diagnosis is wrong, given that it is a sniper bullet that has inflicted this wound?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should perhaps direct the witness to that part in the big box.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where it said that. Perhaps the witness didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Shouldn't be around this third line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, in the large box at the bottom there's a description of what happened. About three lines down, you'll see a word and excuse my pronunciation, "Snajperskim," I think, which I believe I means sniper. That part is talking about the sniper bullet hitting her chest. Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The part of the text that you're talking about, I can see it. I'm just reading this bad Bosnian-Herzegovinian copy just to see what the surgeon, which part of the metal did the surgeon extract from the right side of the chest. Because if it's an explosive wound, a blast wound, it's realistic to expect that the surgeon would extract from the right side area of the chest a shrapnel, or if it's a projectile to extract a part of the projectile or the damaged projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I appreciate that and perhaps I can try to cut that matter short. In the B/C/S you'll see about perhaps 10 to 12 lines down, the words "five cm," for 5 centimetres, and that line reads: "Neurosurgeon noted a gun-shot wound on the right paravertebral of the mid thoracic spine 5 centimetres from the spine." Now, Professor Stankovic, all I'm asking you here is whether, if a doctor -- or, rather, that the doctor has in your opinion used a wrong Latin diagnosis for what they consider a gun-shot wound? Is it your opinion that the diagnosis is incorrect, if this is a gun-shot wound. That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He should have written that it was a gun-shot wound, vulnus sclopetarium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to step back from the examples from these two different doctors using this term to look at a piece of literature. Now, before I do, just a general question: The anthropologist David del Pino testified here and one of the things that he said is that Professor Dr. Vincent Di Maio is really the top researcher and professional in his field, and that's at transcript page 42178. Now, I'm right in saying that Professor Di Maio is a forensic pathologist who specialises in gun-shot wounds. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct in view of the fact that many of us used his textbooks to -- in our studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I saw that Professor Di Maio's book, "Gunshot Wounds" was among the first things that appeared in your reference materials. Did you use that book yourself in your studies, professor, you personally?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my professional activities, I had Professor Di Maio's textbook in my hands several times, and I used it to acquire information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter number 33740A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, what you're going to see is a page from Professor Di Maio's book, "Gunshot Wounds: Practical Aspects of Fire-arms, Ballistics and Forensic Techniques," dated 1999. And on this page, he talks about new ammunition being used through the ages. I'm just going to read the first two lines of this page. It states: "Bone injuries from conical bullets were extremely severe. The term used to described them was explosive." And at that point there is an asterisk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should not leave out the term there "at the time."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Oh, my apologies, Your Honour, let me read that. "Bone injuries from conical bullets were extremely severe. The term used to describe them at the time was explosive." And if we follow the asterisk down to the bottom, Professor Di Maio notes: "In reviewing the literature concerning fire-arms wounds through the age, one is struck by the recurrent use of the term explosive to describe wounds produced by newly introduced weapons or forms of ammunition. This term has been used to describe wounds produced by conical lead bullets, jacketed bullets, hunting bullets, and the M-16." So, Professor Stankovic, it appears that Professor Di Maio in reviewing the literature has found other doctors also using the term explosive to describe injuries inflicted by fire-arms. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the specific case, the first part of the text that you quoted refers to bone, not to soft tissue structures. When you have soft tissue structures, the differences, and I've already spoken about that, the difference between entry wounds with shrapnel or particles of the explosive devices and the projectile are different. They are different --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- other than in cases when --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt but just to let you know I'm -- in this particular example, it is a fleshed body that was struck. So I am talking about flesh injuries inflicted by these guns. Just to make sure we're talking about the same thing. On that basis, it's right to say that it appears that Professor Di Maio has found other doctors who have used the term "explosive" for injuries inflicted by a fire-arm.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's go back to the Srebrenica and Tomasica reports. No expert of The Hague Tribunal did not use the term explosive wounds for a gun-shot wound. Not a single one. They talked about gun-shot wounds and explosive wounds. They did --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- make a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Firstly, this is not in relation to somebody who died at Srebrenica or Tomasica. This is in relation, in fact, to somebody who survived. And I'm -- maybe I can rephrase my question to move this along. I'm not suggesting that your theory on the Latin term is necessarily incorrect. That's not what I'm driving at. All I want to establish for the next part of the discussion is that it appears doctors may have used this Latin term to describe gun-shot wounds even if that was in error, according to you. It's clear that doctors do use this Latin term sometimes to describe gun-shot wounds, regardless of whether that's right or wrong. I take it you would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what Professor Di Maio says, yes, but in the area of the former Yugoslavia, since it was a single school, nobody ever referred to gun-shot wounds as explosive ones. That was not a diagnosis. This something that I assert and it's something that can be verified because we're talking about a document that was written by a professor from the area of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Okay, Professor Stankovic. Now, the document you saw that I showed you first and you saw on Monday, that was actually written in 1995. Now, it's fair to say given what we've seen that the only way to guarantee you understand what the doctor means by that Latin phrase, if the Latin phrase is all you have to go on, the only way to guarantee understanding would actually be to speak to the person who wrote it down and ask them what they meant. That would be the only way to guarantee understanding.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who signed and wrote the medical document would need to show the literature from which they studied and the questions to which they responded, I guess, if they graduated medicine in Sarajevo or Tuzla, they would need to answer questions about the parameters and the knowledge they used to describe an explosive wound, as such, and I know this very well. In the literature, it says gun-shot wounds diagnosis vulnus sclopetarium, explosive wounds are vulnus explosivum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, professor. You're absolutely an expert in this area, and just to reiterate, I'm not driving towards the fact that your description of how it should be used is wrong. The only thing I was trying to establish was that to guarantee understanding, you would have to speak to the doctors. Now, the Prosecution did interview the two doctors who treated the person whose discharge form you saw and you were asked about on Monday and I'd like to show them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we can have a 65 ter 33630.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: What you're going to see on the screen, Professor Stankovic, is the statement of the doctor who treated the patient when he arrived at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This should not be broadcast, Your Honours. And if we can move to the second page in both languages and look at paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It has not been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The number is 33630. The second page in both languages when it is on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, this doctor is describing the entire medical file of this patient. I'd just like to read you a part of it. It's starting in the second line in paragraph 5. And he states: "In this particular case, the description of the injury written in the findings in Latin language, vulnera lacerocontusa, is different from the one written in the file although they were written the same day. The only explanation I can give is that the description in file was written mechanically as explosive wound, vulnera explosiva, which was common term used during the war-time-period for the wartime injuries. In the part where the diagnosis was written besides the comment that the wound was explosive, it was also written that there were remains of the foreign metal object inside the wound. Without actual X-ray picture, I cannot confirm what kind of metal object it was, a shrapnel or a piece of bullet." Now, professor, it seems that this doctor is using this term mechanically rather than having based it on the literature that you've described. And just before you answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think to be fair we should read number 6 as well which relates precisely to that doctor's observations of that, that we're asking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, are you following the suggestion by Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It was coming later on in the next question, but I'm happy to do it now, Your Honour, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Just looking at number 6 there, the doctor states: "At this point I am not able to answer with any certainty what type of injury this was for several reasons. First of all, I am not a forensic expert but a clinical doctor ... second, there is no detailed description of the wound, such as the size, width or the death but only the wounds location, and the most important there is no primary findings of the wound, that is, an examination of the wound shortly after it was inflicted." So, Professor Stankovic, does that first reason, the fact that is he a doctor rather than a forensic expert, that might explain why certainly according to you, he is -- or this term vulnera explosivum has been misused or he doesn't know how to use it possibly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all surgery textbooks that were used for doctors specialising or orthopaedic surgeons, there is a clear description of the differences between blast and explosive wounds. Those who studied in Tuzla did their specialisations at the military medical academy as a rule. So regardless of whether they specialised at the clinic in Sarajevo or the VMA, there is a detailed chapter in surgery textbooks which describe what a gun-shot wound or a blast wound is. Blast wounds are not treated in the same way as gun-shot wounds. Blast wounds cause much more damage on organs and soft tissue in comparison to gun-shot wounds, and they require a very different approach during surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: So we see from the last sentence of paragraph 5 when the doctor says he can't confirm if the piece of metal was shrapnel or a bullet, he clearly doesn't know what's caused this wound and that corresponds to him in his own description simply writing vulnera explosivum mechanically. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would object to the question as phrased because it's not what the doctor says. The doctor says, first of all, he has no recollection of this particular patient in number 3 and he says, without actual X-ray picture, I cannot confirm, which is missing from the question posed by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm happy to include that part in what I read to the doctor. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: So, Professor Stankovic, it's clear from that last sentence what the doctor says, "Without actual X-ray picture, I cannot confirm what kind of metal object it was, a shrapnel or a piece of bullet," that he doesn't know what device caused this injury which corresponds to what he wrote earlier in the paragraph that he can only say that the term vulnera explosivum was written mechanically. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to his statement he used it in a mechanical way, but this way he inflicts a lot of damage to the victim and also causes problems for us because we're discussing something that is actually well known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- I think, Mr. MacDonald, what you intended to do was to draw our attention to the inconsistency sometimes in the language used and sometimes that factual observations are insufficient perhaps to always follow in detail what textbooks may tell you how to diagnosis something. If that was your intention to draw our attention that there's a risk of errors there, then I think you have drawn our attention to that. So if that was your purpose, then I think we could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- certainly that is -- that is a very fair way of summarising the intention but I would like to show Professor Stankovic one more statement from the man who wrote the document he commented upon and after that -- well, I'll do that before the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do that. So you have one -- two minutes left for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we please see 65 ter number 33631. Again, not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, Professor Stankovic, what you're going to see here is the statement by the person who wrote the discharge form that was shown to you on Monday. It's Dr. Zoran Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we can move to page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 5 of the statement we see the name of the patient. I just ask you not to read that out. In paragraph 4, the doctor talks about being shown a document and there's a number there, and I can tell you from that number that's the same document that you were shown. Moving to paragraph 8, this doctor says: "Based on the photo and documents shown to me, I am not able to determine how the wounds were inflicted. The term used in diagnosis in this case, vulnera explosiva, is based on the appearance of the wound, meaning that the tissue of the wound exploded and not that the wound was caused by an explosion." So again, Professor Stankovic, while this doctor has given his reasons why he wrote the term that way, I take it you would disagree that he has used that term correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think to be fair, if we're going to do paragraph 8 we need 4, 5, 6 and 7 which lead up to 8, and which talk about how this doctor has no recollection of the particular patient. And then the rest of the stuff that's there, that also affects his -- because 8 is based upon the photos and the documents shown to me [sic], so we need to know what he has been shown and what he is basing this part of his statement on which is precisely what is in 5, 6, and 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think if you want to further explore that, you can do that in re-examination. It's clear that it's on a limited basis that the statement in paragraph 8 is given. You've done with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd like just for Professor Stankovic to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each person that signs a document stands by it, and the description here is unacceptable. He is signing a document that is later used for the further treatment of the person that was wounded. Now, he does not recollect, he never saw the person, so how could he have written this diagnosis in the first place? This is something that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Stankovic, that's not an answer to the question. The question was were the reasons given as read to you in paragraph 8, whether you would disagree that what -- that he used that term correctly, that in -- in the -- in -- in reading why he did it, that he used a wrong term, in your view. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't doubt that the doctor who provided the statement acted in this way, but I don't understand this behaviour. That's all. I don't have an objection to what he said, that he did as he did. But that's now how one should behave. Now, I can give you some of my assumptions. I don't want to embark on any explanations about things that, to tell you the truth, I don't really understand completely and I don't accept either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll look at the rest of my cross-examination on this point over the break and try to reassess it. But it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for a break. Professor Stankovic, it's time for a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. So if you would follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, one more question about this Latin term. Based on the examples I have shown to you and the literature from Professor Vincent Di Maio, the Prosecution position is that this term, this Latin term, vulnera explosivum can be used in three different situations: That is, wounds inflicted by an explosive device, as you said on Monday; wounds inflicted by a gun; and also used when the doctors are not sure in simply describing the wound. Now, all I'm asking is whether you agree or disagree with the Prosecution position.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with this position of the Prosecution. Only wounds caused by mines and explosives can be diagnosed in Latin as vulnera explosivum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Moving to a separate topic. Now, at transcript page 43367.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And I should say for Your Honours, we're still with the same patient just no longer talking about the Latin. On Tuesday, you testified that 7.62 ammunition was the ammunition of automatic and semi-automatic rifles. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And that ammunition can come copper-jacketed, can't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, you testified at transcript page 43296 to 43297 if it is point blank, a gun-shot injury is probably an entry/exit wound except when it hits a bone, such as the hip bones, which are very thick, and in which a projectile might get stuck. And later on at transcript page 43297, you mention with regard to this particular patient that is the doctor -- sorry, the document you saw on Monday, that pieces of shrapnel tend to get lodged in a much smaller depth. Now, Professor Stankovic, in your experience, have you come across a piece of ammunition, 7.62, where the copper jacket has come away from the core of the bullet when it has hit a human body?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in numerous cases when these bullets hit bones, especially bones that are thick, such as the pelvic bones, the thigh bones, the upper arm bones, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Have you come across examples where the copper jacket has come off and been left in the body when the bullet has only hit a fleshy part of the body, that is, not a bone?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I have come across such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show Professor Stankovic an example of that, and I would like to move through the life of a bullet, so I have here in court a 7.62 bullet that has not been fired, and I'd just like Professor Stankovic to have that, to have access to that so we're discussing the same thing. If Your Honours would like to look at it first, and, of course, my friend, I'm more than happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think every party, and the Bench as well, would like to have a look before it is presented to the witness. You can show it first to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: For the record, I understand that this bullet is registered under 65 ter number 33750.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And, Professor Stankovic, I'm going to ask you to confirm it's a 7.62 round with a copper jacket what we see at the top.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And if -- yes, thank you. Now, I'd like to call up 65 ter 33745 and turn to page 2. Professor Stankovic, this is an autopsy report that you're about to see. It's only in English, so I'm going to read out the parts to you, and on page 2, just for your general information, this is the autopsy report -- this is the autopsy report of a 16-year-old boy, called Jasmin Boric, whose partially skeletonized lower half of body was found in Cancari Road 12, the secondary grave linked to Branjevo farm. Now, I'd like to move to page 4 and at the top this reads: "Recovered objects, projectiles." And the first one is a medium-sized jacket bullet plus distorted jacket adherent to lower end left femur. No boney injury. Now, Professor Stankovic, I have again in court these items taken out of this boy, and I'd like to show them to you, again, for you to comment upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And once, Your Honours, if you would care to see them and my friend Mr. Ivetic, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And, Professor Stankovic, can you confirm that that appears -- and, please, if you hold onto that just for a moment. It appears to be a distorted core of a bullet and the -- sorry. Appears to be the core of a bullet and a distorted copper jacket.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, in -- on the screen, can we move to page 29 and I wonder if we can place page 35 next to it, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And, Professor Stankovic, the photograph on the left is the items that you're holding but taken out and placed next to a ruler. The item on the right is the fluoroscopy, and would you agree with me that it appears we can see the core of the bullet, just underneath the bone there, and to the right and slightly above in front of the bone or adherent to it, as the autopsy report stated, we see the distorted jacket?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could ask that that be taken back. And finally, Professor Stankovic, to go back to our patient who really this discussion is in regard to, the very first document you were shown today, the one you were shown on Monday, I would like to show you an injury -- a photograph of his wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: So if we can have P01440 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And I have the original here for you to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I think the quality is better, Your Honours, so I ask that Your Honours and my friend see it and then Mr. Stankovic have it for his comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder if Professor Stankovic could hold onto that for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 33697 on the screen and page 4 in both languages. Sorry, not to be broadcast, I should have said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, this is the patient explaining to the doctor what happened to him. The first line reads: "Wounded by a bullet in the left hip in Konjevic Polje in 1995 while fleeing an attempted execution." Now, Professor Stankovic, given your testimony that if it is point blank, a gun-shot injury is probably an entry/exit wound except when it hits a bone such as the hip bones which are very thick and in which a projectile might get stuck, as opposed to blast wounds where there are numerous channels that destroy much more soft tissue because the shrapnel has an irregular pattern of penetrating a human body, in the photograph in front of you, would you not agree, in your professional opinion, that that wound is consistent with being shot by a bullet with the smaller entry wound being at the back, the larger exit wound being at the front and that the foreign metal object in the body could be the distorted jacket of the bullet that shot him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please show again the fluoroscope image showing where the segment or fragment of the bullet was found in the body? If you could please show that on the screen once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Sorry, Professor Stankovic, I wasn't clear, clearly, on that. That was simply an example of a bullet passing through the body. We have no fluoroscopy or X-ray for this patient. So knowing that, I wonder if you could give your opinion on the question I asked a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I thought that the previous question was linked with this. If you thought I should then provide an answer to the previous question, whether it's possible for a bullet to be deformed if it only passed through soft tissue, was that the first question? When you showed the bullet that everyone saw, that was distorted. Was that your first question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Sorry. This becomes slightly confused. Undoubtedly my fault. So the bullet that was distorted is to do with another case, not the case of the person whose photograph you're holding just now. That is the photograph of the wound we have for that person [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. But what was the question for the first image? If you can please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: There's no question for the first image. The question is just based on that photograph. Let me ask you: In terms of what you've said, if it -- that -- the wound shown in that photograph, bearing in mind your testimony, which I've read, if that is consistent with a gun-shot wound with the entry at the back and the larger exit wound at the front of the hip?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, this is a scar on the skin with irregular round shape on the border between the left gluteal area and the -- the left waist area, around 20 centimetres to the left and to the front one can notice a bigger scar, perhaps 5 by 2 and a half centimetres in radius, with a darkened skin caved in slightly. Such an injury may be caused by a bullet fired from a hand-held fire-arm which hit the damaged person from the back left side with the channel directed forwards and to the right, and ends at the height of the left outward area of the abdomen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Stankovic. I wonder if we could take that photograph back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move to tender three of the 65 ter numbers I've used before moving on from this discussion. The first two are the two examples. That is -- of the people injured by the sniper. 65 ters 33694 and 33695. And the third one is the note of the doctor about what the patient told him and that is 33697 although I only showed page 4 for that third one, so I'm happy for that to be MFI'd or reserved a number and an excerpt can be made and uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Other pages being irrelevant for us for your --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It's all part of his case file, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have multiple documents, now, where only small snippets shown to the witness, and for some, he's been asked to comment; for some, he's not been asked to comment. So we don't have foundation for the remainder of the documents coming in. I don't know how long they are. I have only seen what's been on the screen since I don't have the full documents before me. But we have the witness's testimony as to what he has been shown. That is relevant but the fact of -- what else is in those documents ... it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you'd prefer to have the excerpt used?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm happy for one page from each document going in, Your Honours, subject to anything that my friend wishes to add or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, fully aware that the witness testified only on certain portions of it, for context if it's not too much if it's only a matter of one or two pages, for context, we'd like to know what it is. So, therefore -- but if they are longer, if it's -- if it's -- five, ten, or fifteen pages, then, of course, we might need an excerpt only and perhaps then the parties should sit together and see whether we need the cover page or whatever, for us to know what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that the first two are two pages, the third one being six pages. I'm happy to sit with Mr. Ivetic for the last one, if Your Honours wish. The one thing I should have added is they should all be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think for the first two, the two-page documents, there seem to be no problems. Mr. Registrar, the numbers would be? And perhaps you repeat what the two-page -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar has some concerns that the two-page documents were shown but perhaps it is the page not shown that causes you to ask them to be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, I was just discussing the same thing with my colleague. In fact the first two do not need to be admitted under seal. It was my mistake. It was only the third one, which I think was not broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then, for the first two ones, the two-page documents and perhaps you repeat the 65 ter number, and then Mr. Registrar then assigns a exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The first two ter numbers are 33694 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay we take it one by one. 33694 receives number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P7816, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7816 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's P7817.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: 33697 under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7818 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that's marked for identification under seal so that you can sit together with Mr. Ivetic and see whether we can do with less pages. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, I'm going to move to an entirely new topic now. I'd like to talk briefly about the principle that you cannot guarantee a cause of death on a body which is skeletonized. And I'd like to look at some autopsies that -- or one autopsy that Dr. Dunjic did in Glodjane in the Decani municipality in September 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33692.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Before we look that specifically, just to make sure we're speaking about the same thing, I understand your position to that if a body is sufficiently skeletonized, you cannot give the cause of death because you cannot say that the injuries were inflicted in life; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And that I think Professor Dunjic is perhaps the most strident about this, that one cannot make an assumption that the injuries were inflicted in life to give the cause of death, that is, I think, one of Professor Dunjic's main criticisms of Dr. Clark; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of the main criticisms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, the witness statement in front of you is from Professor Dunjic, and I'd like to turn to page 48 in the English and page 39 in the B/C/S, and you'll see there a body labelled Re-3, and this relates to the Kosovo cases and the KLA. Now, on this page, we see a summary of where the body was found and when the autopsy was performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we can turn the page, please, in both languages, and we see there the third paragraph: "The body was in an advanced state of decomposition and the cause of death could not be determined by autopsy alone." Now that's the principle that you and I have just agreed, that Professor Dunjic uses to criticise Mr. Clark -- Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, in the next three paragraphs, Professor Dunjic discusses injuries that were found and in the fourth paragraph on this page in English, and two-thirds of the way down the page in the B/C/S, he states: "If these gun-shot wounds to the head and body were inflicted ante-mortem, they were the direct cause of death." Now, what Professor Dunjic has done here is he has provided a cause of death based on an assumption, that assumption being that the gun-shot wounds to the head and body were inflicted in life. That's what he's done, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He's actually asking a question here. Opening up a dilemma. "If these gun-shot wounds to the head and body were inflicted ante-mortem, they were the direct cause of death." What does that mean? He cannot say with any certainty whether the injuries were caused in life or after death, and that's why he allows this possibility, not disputing that the gun-shot wounds to head were a cause of death. If we had such comments in Dr. Clark's report, we could not have had any objections because he just allows the possibility here that the person in charge of the investigation, if he has witness statements or establishes in some other way that the injuries were inflicted in life, that they were then the certain cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we have P02259 on the screen now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, this is Dr. Clark's report on the ICTY operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1999 that you're just about to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd like to look for page 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now it's the second paragraph under number 1. I should say in paragraph 1, Dr. Clark's commenting on the fact that a number -- the majority of the bodies are skeletonized, given how long they had been in the ground. And in this second paragraph, he states: "This brought with it the difficulty of being able to say whether a particular injury had been caused before death, or after it." And skipping a couple of lines, he states: "In decomposed bodies, this becomes extremely difficult, and in skeletonised one, impossible. Strictly speaking therefore, it would never be possible to say, for instance, that a bullet-hole in the skull definitely occurred before death as opposed to after it ..." So, again, this is the principle that you and I agreed and we saw Professor Dunjic included in his statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I am in complete agreement with Dr. Clark's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, in the last paragraph before number 2 on the same page, it states: "In all of the cases therefore, with only occasional exceptions, any injuries suggestive of gun-shot damage were taken to have occurred in life and usually to have been necessarily or potentially fatal." So he's doing the same thing that Professor Dunjic did, in that he's saying, We are assuming that these injuries were caused in life. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is a difference between Professor Dunjic's and Dr. Clark's position. Professor Dunjic stated, if I'm not mistaken, if, which means he is not saying that on the basis of that wound he is drawing a conclusion, but if it's proved that the injury occurred during life, then it can be considered that the gunshot wound was -- to the head was the immediate cause of death. Here it says that any injury indicating damage caused by a bullet would be caused while the person was alive, and then it had to have been or was potentially lethal. But the assertion that it happened during life had to be proved. It is the people who are in charge of the investigation, as you know, who prove this by means of other evidence, such as witness statements and other means, and I already mentioned that. So there is a slight difference in phrasing between the statements of Professor Dunjic and Professor Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I would certainly agree that there's a slight difference in phrasing. And, Professor Stankovic, you were translated there as saying the word that was translated was: "... assertion that it," referring to the gun-shots, "happened during life." You agree with me that Dr. Clark is very clear that this is an assumption that he is making?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's very clear that he is making an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, yesterday at temporary transcript page 31, a portion of Dr. Clark's report pertaining to Kozluk, Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje and Glogova was read to you, stating: "This report is nonetheless compiled on assumption that the vast majority of the gun-shot and other relevant injuries which were found occurred in life and were or contributed to, the cause of death. To assume otherwise would be to make any further analysis of the findings virtually meaningless." And your answer, as it was in the transcript last night was: "I never drew my communications from assumptions and I think that this way of drawing conclusions is unacceptable." So just before we get to the substance, do you recall saying, I would suggest, "I never drew my conclusions from assumptions." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I never, in my life drew any conclusions on the basis of assumptions, either professionally or personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter number 33693, not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, this is a statement you gave to the Tribunal. It was used in the Oric case regarding a victim whose name I won't mention, but you can see it there on the screen in front of you. Now, this was to do with, as you see, Kravica village in early 1993. Am I right in saying that this person was an ethnic Serb?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a man from the village of Kravica whose mortal remains were found in Srebrenica, and the autopsy was carried out on the 7th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to page 3 in both languages, we see the word "Opinion," and the first point there says: "The body of a male exhumed from the soil, in a skeletized state. The autopsy alone cannot establish with certainty the actual cause of death." So this is you, just as Professor Dunjic did, and as Dr. Clark did in his report, repeating this principle?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, if we move to the second point, I'm just going to read it out to you. "On the basis of the appearance and localisation of the bone fractures in the left temporal area of the head, one can make the assumption that death was violent and caused by the destruction and damaging of vital brain centres." So what, in fact, you've done here, Professor Stankovic, is to provide a cause of death based on an assumption, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just assumed in item 2 of the opinion that it -- the death was violent and that it was caused by the destruction and damaging of vie tall brain centre, but I did not assert it. So I said one could make the assumption based on grounds but not assert so. And as to the actual cause of death, that would be something that would be established once the investigating procedure was completed. So I did not assert anything. I just made that assumption, in item 1, the body of a male exhumed from the soil in a skeletized state, the autopsy alone cannot establish with certainty the actual cause of death that is the general position. Then I assumed that the death was violent but I am not asserting that. That is the difference. I am not asserting. I'm just saying that it can be assumed. I am not asserting that the death was violent and all of the rest in view of the position that I stated in item 1 of the relevant opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, if the forensic pathologists who did the thousands of autopsies on bodies and bones from Srebrenica, if each of them had said in their cause of death section, if these wounds were inflicted in life, then they were the direct cause of death, would that then solve the issue that Professor Dunjic raised in his report?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object to the question as being overbroad without specifying which of the particular objections from Professor Dunjic's report are at issue. We've spent several days going over multiple objections, both in relation do Tomasica and to Dr. Dunjic's report, and to give a overly broad one, lumping them all together under one category is neither reflective of the evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, apparently Mr. Ivetic has difficulty in understanding what your question was about. You're invited to pin-point at what point of criticism it is. It could be the one we are discussing already for five minutes but please be clear so that everyone in this courtroom can understand the question without any ambiguity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, with regard to the criticism of Professor Dunjic of Dr. Clark that he makes an assumption regarding the injuries found on the bodies, that assumption being that the wounds were inflicted in life. If the forensic pathologists who did the thousands of autopsies on bodies and bones from Srebrenica, if each of them had said in their cause of death section, If these wounds were inflicted in life, then they were the direct cause of death, would that resolve the -- that particular criticism of Professor Dunjic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it would, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm going to move on from this topic unless Your Honours have any questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, on Monday, at transcript page 43305 to 43306, talking about Dr. Clark, you said: "It is also beyond my understanding that he, as a person who is producing a general report for the ICTY, makes his only photographs. On site, there must have been a scene-of-crimes team from the official authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he could have just pointed and asked them, Please make me photos of this or that body part. I can hardly imagine a forensic pathologist lowering himself to the role of a simple photographer."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, just to make sure that you're correctly transcribed, that question at line 1, 2, 3 -- at line 17, you said "makes his only photographs of." Did you say "only" or "own," makes his own photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I read the transcript yesterday it still had the word "only," I believe. I'm sure that the witness meant "own."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Own. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: So just to finish the quotation, after the words simple photographer, you say: "He is a renowned specialist with great experience." Now, Professor Stankovic, you have performed autopsies where you took your own photographs, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I performed autopsies in areas during combat, I was forced to photograph corpses and everything that was important myself because we did not have a person who could do that, and that is why I made my own photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33702 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This is, again, an ICTY witness statement that you've given, Professor Stankovic. It deals with autopsies you performed in various places in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think you discussed that with my friend Mr. Ivetic on Monday. I'd like to turn to page 23 in the English, page 35 in the B/C/S, and this concerns autopsies you conducted in the Zvornik fire hall on bodies found in Glodjansko Brdo. Now in the second-last paragraph in the English and the first paragraph at the top of the B/C/S, the third sentence states: "I took pictures of all the bodies that I examined." Now, I appreciate that this was in a time of combat, but can you just confirm for me that that's accurate, that in these autopsies, you were taking photographs of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did take my own photographs when I was doing the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page in the English and stay on this page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm looking for the first paragraph. Now, in this paragraph, you say you were assisted by medical technicians, and you name two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And now if -- if we can turn to the next page in the B/C/S, the top paragraph in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And it's the now-next paragraph in the English, reads: "The crime scene technician, Dragomir Damjanovic, was also present. As far as the two technicians, they were helping me with every body that I examined in the fire hall in Zvornik. Damjanovic was mostly always there and he would sometimes help me with the photographing of the bodies and he would take his own photographs of the bodies." Now, Professor Stankovic, I believe a moment ago you said you took photographs in areas of combat because, in essence, there was no one else there to help you. This is a situation where you are a crime-scene technician taking photographs, and you're still taking your own photographs.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see from my statement that mostly he was there all the time and from time to time he would help me to photograph the bodies, and he photographed them himself too. So when he was there, he helped me. When he wasn't there, I photographed the autopsy details. That means that Damjanovic did not have a camera, he did not have any other equipment. He was there as a person who was providing some sort of security for us during our work. He was a crime-scene technician, that's true. He was not from Zvornik. I think he came from Zenica or some other town, and he was assigned to us. But it's true what is said here, that, from time to time, he helped me to photograph, but he did not have his own equipment, and he did not photograph the bodies. There was only one camera that we had that he could use to make photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, Professor Stankovic, in the line I read to you from the previous page, it said you took pictures of all the bodies that you examined, and here we have Mr. Damjanovic taking his own photographs of the bodies. So are you certain that what you're telling the Chamber just now is accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am saying now is correct. I also want to tell you that at other locations where there were no crime-scene technicians those who knew how to take photographs helped us from time to time. And here he also was helping us, as I was performing the autopsy. I would tell him, Take a picture of such and such a part of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, it's not the case that you and Professor Dunjic are -- or have set out to try to criticise Dr. Clark and the others and, in fact, you're criticizing them for things that you yourself have done in the past.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because Dr. Clark performed autopsies or was present during exhumations of graves where there were all possible experts present to be able to help, so you had anthropologists, crime-scene technicians, investigators, and so on and so forth. When we were working in Zvornik, there was shooting around Zvornik and above Zvornik. There was shooting between the warring sides. I went by myself. I had no crime-scene technician help. This person who was there, who happened to be there, was there to provide security for us so it was a person who was working as a crime-scene technician he was helping us, but he was not assigned to the tasks and duties of a crime-scene technician. This is that difference that I'm talking about. We were working in war-torn areas and we had no help from other experts, such as Tomasica. In that case, you had the full range of assistance available, and all the necessary investigative actions were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, this is -- or you don't mention in this statement at all that this person, Dragomir Damjanovic, who, in the statement, is described as a crime-scene technician. It's only now that you're telling the Court that, in fact, he wasn't a crime-scene technician, in fact, he was assigned as security? Is that what you're now saying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was one of the persons who was providing security for the area where we were working, and that was the firemen's hall in Zvornik, who was helping us as a person when we were identifying the mortal remains, he was the one who was bringing in people, family members, close relatives who were looking at the personal items, the clothing. So that was where he was helping us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Time for the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would have -- have you done with this? Yes. Perhaps this would take two or three minutes. I would like to take you back to the post-mortem which you explained and where you emphasised that you assumed that -- let me see ... "that you can make an assumption that death was violent and caused by the destruction and damaging of vital brain centres." And that is 65 ter 33693. Perhaps we could have it on the screen, page 3. And you have clearly explained to us the difference in phrasing you used, that is, you say you can make an assumption, but you do not determine the cause of death. Whereas, Dr. Clark said that I assumed that the injuries were inflicted during life and then comes to establishing causes of death. That's clear what is the difference in your approach of the matter. Now, could I take you here to number V in your opinion, where it says: "It can be assumed with a high degree probability that death was violent." What explains the "high degree probability" that death was violent? Because if I understand you well, it means that you consider it highly probable that the injuries were inflicted during life. Where is that probability, what -- on what is that based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not highly probable. It says there is a good basis for this. So it could happen, it's possible but it does not necessarily have to be so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes. Now, in English, it reads, and if you say that's not a correct translation, it reads: "It can be assumed with high degree probability," that's for me a high probability. It's not, there is a possibility but, in English, it says, There is a high degree probability. Is that an accurate translation of what you used as language in your original report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be assumed based on -- it -- good foundations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are grounds to assume this: Osnovano pretpostaviti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then, perhaps that specific language, we'll have that verified over the break so that we know that -- whether we are dealing with a translation issue or whether I have a relevant question for you. We take that break first. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The verification of point V in the opinion is not there yet, so if you move on, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: To save time, Your Honours, perhaps I could ask for the next exhibit to be brought on to the screen. It's P07443.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I also emphasise that it often helps the Chamber already very much to know what the dispute is and that sometimes the final answer to it might not be expected necessarily from a witness but it includes often an evaluation of other elements of the evidence as well, and that if the issue is clear to us that that is already of great assistance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, going back to one of the criticisms you made of Dr. Clark in the -- in his Tomasica report, we have his Tomasica report in front of us, I think, P07443.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's apparently not what we have before us at this moment. And now perhaps in the English. Yep. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: We're looking for page 6 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S.
